title: Development of Law in the Middle Ages

2.title: Development of the Law in the Middle Ages

3.title: The Migration Period (4th–6th century)
3.text: The same map as in the previous lecture: Saxons, Franks, Alemanni, Bavarians, Visigoths, and the Vandals and Ostrogoths whom Justinian later defeated. It is the starting position for everything that follows.

4.title: A barbarian invasion?
4.text: The answer the lecture gives is no. There was no 'vandalism' in the modern sense but a GRADUAL TRANSFORMATION of the Roman Empire, and the church acted as the mediator between antiquity and the Middle Ages — it carried Roman administration, Roman language and Roman law across the break. The word vandalism is itself a later polemic against a people, not a description of what happened.

cards.q: Was the end of the Roman Empire in the West a barbarian invasion?
cards.a: Not in the sense of destruction: the lecture describes a gradual transformation of the Roman Empire, with the church acting as mediator between antiquity and the Middle Ages and carrying Roman law and administration across the break.

5.title: The leges barbarorum on the map
5.text: Where each of the Germanic law codes applied: Lex Saxonum in the north, the Frankish leges (Lex Salica, Lex Ribuaria), Lex Alemannorum, Lex Bavariorum, Lex Visigothorum in the south-west.

6.title: What the leges barbarorum are made of
6.text: Three streams flow into them: post-classical Roman law in its simplified form, VULGAR LAW; Christianity; and Germanic law. So a lex barbarorum is not a pure Germanic text but a mixture, written in Latin, under Christian influence, on a late-Roman substrate. The slide's example shows how to read such a text: the permitted killing of one's own children was widespread in most pre-Christian cultures, and the fact that the leges PROHIBIT it testifies to how practically important the practice still was. A prohibition is evidence that the thing prohibited was happening.

terms.def: Post-classical Roman law in simplified, practice-worn form, as it survived in the provinces. One of the three ingredients of the leges barbarorum.

cards.q: Which three currents feed into the leges barbarorum?
cards.a: Post-classical Roman law in its simplified form (vulgar law), Christianity, and Germanic law. They are mixtures written in Latin, not pure Germanic texts.

cards.q: What does the prohibition of killing one's own children in the leges barbarorum tell a legal historian?
cards.a: That the practice was still widespread and practically important. A rule is enacted against what actually happens — the prohibition is evidence of the conduct, not of its absence.

7.title: The leges barbarorum: who wrote what, and when
7.text: First to record their own law were the Visigoths in southern France and Spain: the Edictum Theodorici of 459 and the Codex Euricianus of 476. In the area of present-day Austria it is the Alemanni and Bavarians: Lex Alamannorum 725, Lex Baiuvariorum 740. The youngest of them is the Lex Saxonum of 802 — and note who enacted it: the Frankish king Charlemagne, AFTER subjugating the Saxons. A conquered people receiving its 'own' law from the conqueror. Some Germanic kings also enacted Roman law for their Roman subjects, for instance the Lex Romana Visigothorum of 506.

terms.def: Roman law enacted by a Germanic king for his Roman subjects — an example of personality of law: which law applied depended on who you were.

cards.q: Who recorded their law first among the Germanic peoples, and which is the youngest of the leges barbarorum?
cards.a: First the Visigoths in southern France and Spain — Edictum Theodorici 459, Codex Euricianus 476. Youngest is the Lex Saxonum of 802, enacted by Charlemagne after he had subjugated the Saxons.

cards.q: Which leges barbarorum applied in the area of present-day Austria, and when?
cards.a: The Lex Alamannorum of 725 and the Lex Baiuvariorum of 740 — the laws of the Alemanni and the Bavarians.

8.title: Where the leges mattered — and where they did not
8.text: The lasting effect was in the Romance territories, mainly Spain. In the areas where the German language developed — present-day Austria among them — they had barely any practical implications. France ends up split down the middle by this: written law in the Romance south, orally handed-down customary law in the north. That division of France into pays de droit écrit and pays de droit coutumier survives until the Code civil, and it is worth remembering now because the course returns to it.

cards.q: Where did the leges barbarorum have a lasting effect, and where almost none?
cards.a: Lasting effect in the Romance territories, mainly Spain. Almost none where the German language developed, such as present-day Austria. France was split: written law in the Romance south, oral customary law in the north.

9.title: Charlemagne and the two-emperors problem
9.text: The Frankish kingdom expands across central Europe, and the Pope crowns Charlemagne Emperor. That creates the TWO-EMPERORS PROBLEM: there is now an emperor in the west and an emperor in Byzantium, each claiming to be THE Roman emperor, and the Roman empire was by definition one. The problem is not academic — it is about who is the legitimate continuation of Rome, and it shapes relations between west and east for centuries.

terms.def: After Charlemagne's imperial coronation there are two claimants to the one Roman imperial dignity, in the west and in Byzantium. The Roman empire was by definition singular, so both could not be right.

cards.q: What is the 'two-emperors problem' and what creates it?
cards.a: Charlemagne's coronation as Emperor by the Pope. There is then an emperor in the west and an emperor in Byzantium, each claiming the one Roman imperial dignity — which by definition could not be held twice.

10.title: The imperial title again
10.text: The genealogy from the introductory lecture, repeated here because Charlemagne's coronation is the moment the western branch begins: Roman-German Emperor 800/962–1806, beside the Byzantine Emperor to 1453, and later the Russian Tsar, the Ottoman Sultan, the Emperor of the French, the German and the Austrian Emperor.

11.title: The two swords doctrine
11.text: Compare three answers to the same question — who holds spiritual and who temporal power. The CALIPH is both the spiritual and the temporal head of the Muslims. The BYZANTINE EMPEROR rules the imperial church of Byzantium, so the temporal ruler holds the spiritual power too. In the OCCIDENT, and only there, the Pope is able to assert himself as AT LEAST EQUAL to the emperor. Two swords, two hands: that separation is a peculiarity of western Europe, and much of European constitutional history — investiture contest, church and state, secularisation — follows from it.

terms.def: The western separation of spiritual and temporal power into two hands — Pope and Emperor — as against the caliph and the Byzantine emperor, each of whom held both.

cards.q: What is the two swords doctrine, and what makes the western answer unusual?
cards.a: That spiritual and temporal power are held in two separate hands. The caliph was spiritual and temporal head of the Muslims; the Byzantine emperor ruled the imperial church. Only in the Occident did the Pope assert himself as at least equal to the emperor — a separation which shapes later European constitutional history.

12.title: The social order: classes defined by legal status
12.text: The definition is legal, not economic: a SOCIAL CLASS is a group of people who differ from other classes because of their different LEGAL STATUS. Nobility, bourgeoisie, peasantry. The Sachsenspiegel illustration on the slide shows those groups placed under the special protection of the king — monks, secular priests, married and unmarried women, and Jews. Different status means different law, not merely different wealth.

terms.def: A group of people who differ from other classes by their different LEGAL STATUS — nobility, bourgeoisie, peasantry. A legal, not an economic category.

cards.q: How does the lecture define a social class in the Middle Ages, and why does the definition matter?
cards.a: As a group differing from other classes by its LEGAL STATUS — nobility, bourgeoisie, peasantry. It matters because status decided which law applied to a person, not merely how rich they were.

cards.q: Which groups does the Sachsenspiegel show under the special protection of the king?
cards.a: Monks, secular priests, married and unmarried women, and Jews.

13.title: Feudalism: rule over land is rule over people
13.text: The economic base first: agricultural structures, 90 per cent of people are peasants, with subsistence farming and barter trade predominating. A small aristocratic upper class exercises power, and the formula to remember is that RULE OVER LAND MEANS RULE OVER PEOPLE. The decisive factor is physical proximity: the landlord nearby matters far more than the king far away. That is why medieval power looks fragmented — it is exercised at walking distance.

cards.q: What does 'rule over land means rule over people' mean, and why was the nearby landlord more important than the king?
cards.a: That holding land carried public authority over those who lived on it. In a world of subsistence farming, where 90 per cent were peasants, power was exercised at walking distance — the landlord nearby could actually reach you, the king far away could not.

14.title: Why feudalism is not just wealth
14.text: The lecture's own test: today, even if Elon Musk bought all the land in Austria, the Chancellor would still be the Chancellor. In the age of feudalism that was NOT so — private land ownership and public rule over territory were linked indivisibly. The modern separation of property from sovereignty, which we take for granted, is exactly what feudalism lacked, and building that separation is one of the things the rest of this course describes.

cards.q: Buying all the land in a country today would not make you its ruler. Why would it have, under feudalism?
cards.a: Because private land ownership and public rule over territory were linked indivisibly — land carried authority with it. The modern separation of property from sovereignty did not yet exist.

15.title: Manorialism
15.text: Central Europe stays mainly agrarian into the 19th century. Peasants were dependent on the landlord — the lord of the manor, who might be a secular or ecclesiastical noble, a monastery, a town, occasionally a prince or a king. The dependency was threefold: in personal rights, in property rights, and in political authority. And it formed a distinct legal circle of its own, the LEX FAMILIAE — the law of the manorial household.

terms.def: The law of the manorial household — the narrowest of the medieval legal circles, governing the lord and his dependent peasants.

cards.q: In what three respects were peasants dependent on the lord of the manor, and who could be such a lord?
cards.a: In personal rights, in property rights and in political authority. The lord could be a secular or ecclesiastical noble, a monastery, a town, occasionally a prince or king. The law of that relationship was the lex familiae.

16.title: The manor in plan
16.text: The diagram of a manor: the demesne, worked for the lord; the tenured land, held by peasants; and the forest as commons.

17.title: West and east: tenured land against demesne
17.text: The same institution produces opposite conditions depending on which part dominates. In WESTERN AND CENTRAL EUROPE tenured land prevails: peasants pay dues and their personal legal status is only slightly restricted. In EASTERN EUROPE the demesne prevails: peasants have very little land of their own and are completely dependent on the landlord — SERFDOM. The lord grants land, gives consent when a peasant wishes to marry, and exercises jurisdiction over his peasants; a peasant only comes into contact with the king or prince when accused of a capital crime, where a death sentence is at stake.

terms.def: The part of the manor worked directly for the lord. Where it predominates — eastern Europe — the peasants hold almost nothing of their own and fall into serfdom.
Land held by peasants against dues. Where it predominates — western and central Europe — the peasants' personal status is only slightly restricted.

cards.q: Why did manorialism produce serfdom in eastern Europe but not in the west?
cards.a: Because of which part of the manor dominated. In the west and centre tenured land prevailed: peasants paid dues and kept a largely free personal status. In the east the demesne prevailed: peasants had almost no land of their own and became completely dependent — serfdom.

cards.q: When did a medieval peasant come into contact with the king or prince rather than his landlord?
cards.a: Only when accused of a capital crime, where a death sentence was at stake. Otherwise the lord granted his land, consented to his marriage and exercised jurisdiction over him.

18.title: The end of manorialism
18.text: The absolutist state wanted access to ALL its subjects, so it tried to bring manorial courts under its control and to limit the lords' jurisdiction — but it did not abolish manorialism. Manorialism therefore remains the main source of aristocratic power well into the 19th century. Abolition, when it comes, differs by country: PRUSSIA 1811, where the land is divided between landlord and peasants; AUSTRIA 1848, where peasants are given title to their holdings and the landlords are compensated through bonds.

cards.q: How and when was manorialism abolished in Prussia and in Austria?
cards.a: Prussia 1811: the land was divided between landlord and peasants. Austria 1848: peasants were given title to their holdings and the landlords were compensated through bonds.

cards.q: What did the absolutist state do about manorialism, and what did it NOT do?
cards.a: It tried to bring manorial courts under state control and to limit the lords' jurisdiction, because it wanted access to every subject. It did not abolish manorialism, which stayed the main source of aristocratic power into the 19th century.

19.title: Manorialism and feudalism compared
19.text: The comparison the exam wants. WHAT THEY SHARE: lending land creates a personal bond — between landlord and peasant, or between feudal lord and vassal. HOW THEY DIFFER: vassals were NOBLEMEN, and their service could not be of a menial nature — it was auxilium, assistance in arms, and consilium, advice. And vassals could pass fiefs on to their own vassals, which produces the FEUDAL PYRAMID. A peasant's dependency ends with him; a vassal's can be relayed downwards. The slide's example is Frederick Barbarossa enfeoffing Henry the Babenberg with the Duchy of Austria in 1156.

terms.def: The two services a vassal owed: assistance in arms and advice. Never menial work — that is what separates a vassal from a dependent peasant.
The layered structure arising because a vassal could enfeoff vassals of his own, passing land and obligation downwards.

cards.q: What do manorialism and feudalism have in common, and what separates them?
cards.a: Both create a personal bond through the lending of land — lord and peasant, or feudal lord and vassal. They differ in that vassals were noblemen whose service could not be menial (auxilium, assistance in arms, and consilium, advice), and that vassals could pass fiefs to their own vassals, producing the feudal pyramid.

cards.q: What happened in 1156 in Austria, and what kind of act was it?
cards.a: Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa enfeoffed Henry the Babenberg with the Duchy of Austria — an act of feudal law, and the beginning of Austria as a territorial duchy.

20.title: The feudal pyramid
20.text: The pyramid drawn out: king at the top, then the great vassals, then their vassals, down to the knights — each layer holding from the one above and granting to the one below.

21.title: Municipal law as the driving force
21.text: Some towns were able to free themselves from the town's lord; they were granted town privileges or adopted statutes of their own. Municipal law is far more DYNAMIC than the lex familiae, because it has to answer questions the manor never asks: remote trade, contracts with craftsmen and artists, credit. That is why the lecture calls municipal law the driving force behind the development of medieval law — the pressure for new law comes from the towns.

cards.q: Why does the lecture call municipal law the driving force of medieval legal development?
cards.a: Because towns faced problems the manor never posed — long-distance trade, contracts with craftsmen, credit — so their law had to be far more dynamic than the lex familiae. New law was made where new questions arose.

22.title: Municipal law families
22.text: From the 10th century German settlers founded new towns, and a new town would take over the law of a MOTHER TOWN — creating a law family. The most important are the families of MAGDEBURG and LÜBECK. The mechanism is worth seeing for what it is: law spreading by adoption rather than by conquest or legislation, and a town keeping legal ties to a mother town far away, including appeals to it on doubtful questions.

terms.def: A group of towns sharing the law of one mother town, which they adopted at foundation. The two great families are Magdeburg and Lübeck.

cards.q: What is a municipal law family and which are the two most important?
cards.a: A group of towns that took over the law of a mother town at their foundation, mostly newly founded by German settlers from the 10th century on. The most important families are Magdeburg and Lübeck.

23.title: Legal circles and the rule that resolves them
23.text: Territorial rule replaces tribal associations — Austria in 1156 is the example. Within a territory several bodies of law apply at once: imperial law, land law, municipal law, and the rural lex familiae (Hofrecht). The rule that sorts them out is the one to memorise: THE NARROWER LEGAL CIRCLE TAKES PRECEDENCE OVER THE WIDER. The result is fragmentation — a multitude of different bodies of law, each valid in its own circle, with the closest one winning.

terms.def: One of the concentric bodies of law valid in a medieval territory — imperial law, land law, municipal law, lex familiae. The narrower circle takes precedence over the wider.

cards.q: Name the medieval legal circles and the rule for conflicts between them.
cards.a: Imperial law, land law, municipal law and the rural lex familiae (Hofrecht). The narrower legal circle takes precedence over the wider — the closest law wins.

cards.q: Why was medieval law fragmented rather than unified?
cards.a: Because territorial rule replaced tribal associations and each territory carried several legal circles at once, each valid in its own sphere, with the narrower prevailing over the wider. There was no single body of law to displace them.

24.title: Law books: the Sachsenspiegel and the Schwabenspiegel
24.text: A medieval law book is NOT legislation. It is a private recording of customary law — a reflection of the law in place, not an enactment of it. Some nevertheless came to have the same effect as actual laws, and all of them give an authentic image of medieval customary law. The best known are the Sachsenspiegel, the Saxon Mirror, of around 1225, and the Schwabenspiegel, the Swabian Mirror. Getting this distinction right is worth a mark: a Spiegel is a mirror, and it says so in its own name.

terms.def: A private recording of customary law, not an enactment. The Sachsenspiegel (c. 1225) and Schwabenspiegel are the best known; some acquired law-like effect in practice.

cards.q: Is the Sachsenspiegel a statute?
cards.a: No. It is a law book — a private recording of customary law, reflecting the law in place rather than enacting it (around 1225). Some law books nevertheless came to have the same effect as actual laws, and they are our most authentic image of medieval customary law.

25.title: Written legal culture
25.text: From the 14th century more and more legal transactions are written down, and the consequences are institutional. A new profession appears: the NOTARY. Form books collect the wording of recurring transactions. And registers of legal transactions are kept — the precursor of the modern land register, and, the slide notes, UNKNOWN IN ROMAN LAW. An early precursor is the Domesday Book of 1086, recording land ownership in England; Vienna's own example is the Eisenbuch, the 'iron book', holding the city's legal transactions from the 14th to the 18th century.

terms.def: The medieval precursor of the land register: a public book recording transactions. Roman law knew nothing like it — this is a genuinely medieval invention.

cards.q: What did the spread of written legal transactions from the 14th century bring with it?
cards.a: A new profession, the notary; form books for recurring transactions; and registers of legal transactions — the precursor of the modern land register, which Roman law did not know. Vienna's example is the Eisenbuch (14th–18th century), an earlier one is the Domesday Book of 1086.

cards.q: Which central institution of modern property law has no Roman ancestor?
cards.a: The land register. It grows out of the medieval registers of legal transactions and was unknown in Roman law.

27.title: The seven liberal arts
27.text: Teaching happens in monastic and cathedral schools, training priests at first and gradually other professions too. The curriculum is the septem artes liberales in two groups. TRIVIUM: grammar, rhetoric (the art of oratory), dialectic (logic). QUADRIVIUM: arithmetic, geometry, astrology (astronomy), music (theory). The trivium is the lawyer's half — a medieval jurist is trained first to read a text closely, argue it and detect contradiction, which is exactly what the scholastic method then does to legal sources.

terms.def: Grammar, rhetoric and dialectic — the verbal arts. The training that makes the scholastic treatment of legal texts possible.
Arithmetic, geometry, astrology (astronomy) and music theory — the mathematical arts.

cards.q: Name the seven liberal arts in their two groups.
cards.a: Trivium: grammar, rhetoric (oratory), dialectic (logic). Quadrivium: arithmetic, geometry, astrology (astronomy), music theory.

28.title: The medieval universities
28.text: A growing influx of students from the 11th century leads to the founding of 'communities of teachers and students' — universitates magistrorum et scholarium. That is what a university originally IS: a corporation of people, not a set of buildings. Bologna in the 11th century, Paris (the Sorbonne) in the 13th. Then a second wave founded for POLITICAL reasons: Prague 1348, Cracow 1364, Vienna 1365.

terms.def: 'Community of teachers and students' — the original meaning of university: a corporation of persons, not an institution of the state or the church.

cards.q: What does 'universitas' originally mean, and when were Bologna, Prague, Cracow and Vienna founded?
cards.a: A universitas magistrorum et scholarium is a community of teachers and students — a corporation of persons. Bologna in the 11th century, Paris (Sorbonne) in the 13th; then foundations for political reasons: Prague 1348, Cracow 1364, Vienna 1365.

29.title: University autonomy
29.text: Universities were NOT under the authority of an abbot or a bishop — they were autonomous, and that autonomy is their defining feature against the older monastic and cathedral schools. It lasted a long time: it was only around 1750 that Maria Theresa transformed the autonomous universities into STATE institutions. Latin was taught at all of them, and contacts between the universities of Europe were close — a shared language and a shared curriculum made a European scholarly space long before there was a European polity.

cards.q: What distinguished the medieval university from a monastic or cathedral school, and when did that change in Austria?
cards.a: Autonomy: it was not under the authority of an abbot or bishop. Around 1750 Maria Theresa turned the autonomous universities into state institutions.

cards.q: What made a European scholarly space possible before there was a European polity?
cards.a: Latin taught at every university and close contacts between them — a shared language and a shared curriculum meant a scholar or a legal doctrine could move across Europe.

30.title: Four faculties, two laws
30.text: The medieval university has four faculties: arts (the septem artes liberales), theology, law and medicine. The law faculty studies TWO laws: ecclesiastical law, canonistics, and secular law, legistics. Master both and you are a doctor iuris utriusque — doctor of both laws. The title still survives, and it records the fact that a medieval lawyer had two systems to know, not one.

terms.def: Doctor of both laws — canon (ecclesiastical) and civil (secular). The medieval law faculty taught both.

cards.q: Which two laws did the medieval law faculty teach, and what was the resulting title?
cards.a: Canonistics, the study of ecclesiastical (canon) law, and legistics, the study of secular law. Mastering both made one a doctor iuris utriusque — doctor of both laws.

31.title: Canonistics
31.text: A canon is a rule; canon law is (Catholic) church law. It applies partly only to clerics and partly to laymen as well. Its sources are the Bible, the decisions of the various councils and synods, papal decisions (decretals) and more. And it carries a rule of great consequence for the survival of Roman law: ROMAN LAW APPLIES SUBSIDIARILY — 'ecclesia vivit lege romana', the church lives by Roman law. Through the church, Roman law stayed in use even where no Roman state remained.

terms.def: 'The church lives by Roman law' — Roman law applies subsidiarily within canon law. One of the main routes by which Roman law survived the Middle Ages.
A papal decision serving as a source of canon law.

cards.q: What are the sources of canon law, and what does 'ecclesia vivit lege romana' mean?
cards.a: The Bible, decisions of councils and synods, papal decisions (decretals) and others. 'The church lives by Roman law' states that Roman law applies subsidiarily in canon law — one of the main ways Roman law survived when no Roman state did.

32.title: The Decretum Gratiani
32.text: Gratian, a monk in northern Italy at Bologna, around 1140. His work's real title states its method: CONCORDIA DISCORDANTIUM CANONUM, the harmony of discordant canons — a coherent and comprehensive account of canon law assembled out of texts that contradict each other. The method is SCHOLASTICISM: contradictions are exposed as merely apparent and resolved by distinction. It superseded the older collections and acquired law-like significance, and the jurists who then worked on it scholarly are the DECRETISTS.

terms.def: Gratian's 'concordia discordantium canonum' (c. 1140, Bologna): canon law assembled into a coherent whole by scholastic resolution of contradictions. Superseded older collections and acquired law-like force.
The method of exposing contradictions between authoritative texts as merely apparent and resolving them by distinction — used on canon law by Gratian and on the Digest by the glossators.
The jurists who worked scholarly on the Decretum Gratiani.

cards.q: What is the Decretum Gratiani and what method does its title describe?
cards.a: Gratian's coherent and comprehensive account of canon law, written at Bologna around 1140. Its title — concordia discordantium canonum, the harmony of discordant canons — names the scholastic method: contradictions between authorities are exposed as merely apparent and resolved by distinction.

cards.q: Who are the decretists and who are the decretalists?
cards.a: Decretists work scholarly on the Decretum Gratiani. Decretalists are the later school treating the decretals — the papal law-making of the 13th century.

33.title: Canon law after Gratian
33.text: The 13th century is the age of prolific papal law-making — the decretals — and the DECRETALISTS are the school that treats them scholarly. The official collections follow: the Liber Extra in 1234, the Liber Sextus in 1298, the Clementinae in 1317, named after Pope Clement V. Then the decline of the papacy in the late Middle Ages, the Reformation, and the Council of Trent 1545–1563. The collections are finally gathered as the Corpus Iuris Canonici in 1582, replaced by the Codex Iuris Canonici in 1917 and again in 1983 — canon law is still living law, with a code younger than most civil codes.

cards.q: Name the collections of canon law in order, from the 13th century to today.
cards.a: Liber Extra 1234, Liber Sextus 1298, Clementinae 1317 (after Clement V), gathered as the Corpus Iuris Canonici in 1582; then the Codex Iuris Canonici of 1917, replaced by that of 1983.

34.title: Legistics and the rediscovery of the Digest
34.text: Legistics is the study of secular law, the leges. Its home is northern Italy, Lombardy — the centre of the Lombard kingdom — with the law schools of Pavia and Bologna. The event that starts everything is the discovery around 1155 of a manuscript of the DIGEST, the Codex Florentinus. Justinian's collection of classical jurisprudence, largely unused in the west for centuries, is suddenly available as a text to be studied. That single manuscript is the beginning of the European science of law.

terms.def: The manuscript of Justinian's Digest discovered around 1155 in northern Italy — the text on which the glossators founded the European science of law.

cards.q: What is legistics, where was it practised, and what discovery set it going?
cards.a: The study of secular law (leges), practised in northern Italy — Lombardy, at the law schools of Pavia and Bologna. It was set going by the discovery around 1155 of a manuscript of Justinian's Digest, the Codex Florentinus.

35.title: The glossators
35.text: IRNERIUS, around 1130, was the first to treat the Digest scholarly. The method is again scholasticism, and the attitude is the key to the whole school: NO DOUBT IS RAISED ABOUT THE AUTHORITY OF THE TEXT — and yet the law develops further, HIDDEN inside the work of explaining it. A gloss is an explanation of the legal text, written in the margin (marginal gloss) or between the lines (interlinear gloss). Formally the glossators only explain; substantively they build a new law inside the old text.

terms.def: An explanation of a legal text written in the margin (marginal) or between the lines (interlinear). The glossators' form of work.
Around 1130 the first to treat Justinian's Digest scholarly, at Bologna — the founder of the school of glossators.

cards.q: How did the glossators work, and what is the paradox in their method?
cards.a: They wrote glosses — explanations in the margin or between the lines — on the Digest, using the scholastic method. The paradox: they never questioned the authority of the text, yet the law developed further in a hidden way inside the work of explaining it.

cards.q: Who founded the school of glossators, and when?
cards.a: Irnerius, around 1130, who was the first to treat the Digest in a scholarly way.

36.title: A glossed page
36.text: The layout itself makes the method visible: the Digest text in the middle of the page, the glossa wrapped around it.

37.title: The glossators at work — and the Glossa ordinaria
37.text: Their genres: introductory texts (introductiones) and summaries (summae). Irnerius had four famous students, the QUATTUOR DOCTORES — Bulgarus, Martinus, Jacobus and Hugo — who gave a legal opinion at the Assembly of Roncaglia in 1158, jurists advising an emperor on the basis of Roman texts. The school culminates in FRANCISCUS ACCURSIUS and his Glossa ordinaria of around 1230, roughly 97,000 glosses, which became the standard apparatus. Hence the saying: 'Quidquid non agnoscit glossa, non agnoscit curia' — what the gloss does not recognise, the court does not recognise. The gloss, not the ancient text alone, is what is actually applied.

terms.def: Accursius' standard apparatus of glosses, around 1230, roughly 97,000 glosses. It became the authoritative reading of the Corpus Iuris.
Irnerius' four students — Bulgarus, Martinus, Jacobus, Hugo — who gave the legal opinion at the Assembly of Roncaglia in 1158.

cards.q: What does 'quidquid non agnoscit glossa, non agnoscit curia' mean, and what does it show?
cards.a: 'What the gloss does not recognise, the court does not recognise.' It shows that what was actually applied was not the ancient text alone but the text as read through Accursius' Glossa ordinaria (c. 1230, some 97,000 glosses).

cards.q: Who were the quattuor doctores and what are they known for?
cards.a: Bulgarus, Martinus, Jacobus and Hugo, the four students of Irnerius. They gave the legal opinion at the Assembly of Roncaglia in 1158.

38.title: The commentators
38.text: After Accursius there are no more glossators, and the school that follows carries three names for the same people, each naming a different aspect. POST-GLOSSATORS, because they come after the glossators. COMMENTATORS, because their main genre is now the commentary rather than the gloss. CONSILIATORS, because they give legal opinions — consilia — on actual cases. The important names are BARTOLUS DE SASSOFERRATO and BALDUS DE UBALDIS. Their lasting achievement is the STATUTE THEORY, the first step towards rules on conflict of laws: with a multitude of city statutes beside the common Roman law, someone had to work out which statute governs which case.

terms.def: The commentators' doctrine deciding which of several city statutes applies to a case — the first step towards modern conflict-of-laws rules.
Legal opinions on actual cases, the genre that gives the commentators their third name, consiliators.

cards.q: Why are the commentators called post-glossators, commentators AND consiliators?
cards.a: Post-glossators because they come after Accursius, when glossing stops; commentators because their main genre becomes the commentary; consiliators because they give legal opinions (consilia) on real cases. Three names, one school — Bartolus de Sassoferrato and Baldus de Ubaldis are the great names.

cards.q: What is the statute theory and why was it needed?
cards.a: The commentators' doctrine determining which of the many city statutes governs a given case, alongside the common Roman law. It is the first step towards conflict-of-laws rules, and it was needed because legal fragmentation made the question of the applicable law unavoidable.
